claim: Myosin 5a is a dual-headed molecular motor that transports cargo along actin filaments.
source: Myosin 5a is a dual-headed molecular motor that transports cargo along actin filaments.
evidence: This is a foundational statement in the abstract that draws from established scientific knowledge about myosin 5a function.

claim: The detached head occupies a loosely fixed position to one side of actin from which it rebinds in a controlled manner while executing a step.
source: By following the motion of individual heads with interferometric scattering microscopy at nm spatial and ms temporal precision we found that the detached head occupies a loosely fixed position to one side of actin from which it rebinds in a controlled manner while executing a step.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations using interferometric scattering microscopy as described in the abstract and detailed in the Results section.

claim: Sub-nm spatial precision provided evidence for an ångstrom-level structural transition in the motor domain associated with the power stroke.
source: Improving the spatial precision to the sub-nm regime provided evidence for an ångstrom-level structural transition in the motor domain associated with the power stroke.
evidence: This claim is based on experimental data obtained at improved spatial precision as described in the abstract and Results section.

claim: Consecutive steps follow identical paths to the same side of actin in a compass-like spinning motion demonstrating a symmetrical walking pattern.
source: Simultaneous tracking of both heads revealed that consecutive steps follow identical paths to the same side of actin in a compass-like spinning motion demonstrating a symmetrical walking pattern.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from simultaneous tracking of both heads as described in the abstract and Results section.

claim: Myosin 5a moves in a hand-over-hand fashion with individual heads moving by 74 nm and the center of mass by 37 nm for each step.
source: Myosin 5a moves in a hand-over-hand fashion with individual heads moving by 74 nm and the center of mass by 37 nm for each step (Vale, 2003; Sellers and Veigel, 2006; Hammer and Sellers, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: A finely tuned kinetic sequence of ATP binding, hydrolysis, phosphate release and eventually ADP release by the enzymatic heads enables processive motion towards the '+' end of actin filaments.
source: A finely tuned kinetic sequence of ATP binding, hydrolysis, phosphate release and eventually ADP release by the enzymatic heads enables processive motion towards the '+' end of actin filaments (De La Cruz et al., 1999; De La Cruz and Ostap, 2004; Rosenfeld and Sweeney, 2004; Sakamoto et al., 2008; Forgacs et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous literature.

claim: Crystal structures of myosin 5a exist either with or without nucleotide, but only in the detached state.
source: Crystal structures of myosin 5a exist either with or without nucleotide, but only in the detached state (Coureux et al., 2003, 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to crystal structure studies.

claim: The internally coupled rearrangement of the subdomains leading to ADP and phosphate release or dissociation from actin upon ATP binding could only be studied in silico.
source: Although these structures served as a model for the structural changes potentially induced by binding to actin, (Volkmann et al., 2005) the internally coupled rearrangement of the subdomains leading to ADP and phosphate release or dissociation from actin upon ATP binding could only be studied in silico (Cecchini et al., 2008, 2010; Sweeney and Houdusse, 2010; Preller and Holmes, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to computational studies.

claim: Single molecule studies employing optical trapping and fluorescence imaging have either reported periods of increased flexibility or partitioning of the step into sub-events.
source: Single molecule studies employing optical trapping (Mehta et al., 1999; Rief et al., 2000) and fluorescence imaging (Forkey et al., 2003; Yildiz et al., 2003; Snyder et al., 2004; Warshaw et al., 2005) have either reported periods of increased flexibility, (Veigel et al., 2002; Dunn and Spudich, 2007; Beausang et al., 2013) or partitioning of the step into sub-events (Veigel et al., 2002; Uemura et al., 2004; Cappello et al., 2007; Sellers and Veigel, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous single molecule studies.

claim: All resulting models involve a forward aiming power stroke followed by a Brownian search mechanism.
source: All resulting models involve a forward aiming power stroke followed by a Brownian search mechanism (Veigel et al., 2002; Okada et al., 2007; Shiroguchi and Kinosita, 2007; Karagiannis et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous modeling studies.

claim: The power stroke of the attached head contributes only partially to the step by moving the pivot point that facilitates Brownian rotation of the unbound head.
source: The power stroke of the attached head contributes only partially to the step by moving the pivot point that facilitates Brownian rotation of the unbound head.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from previous models and studies.

claim: The first passage time of the translocating head is expected to be on the order of 100 µs.
source: The first passage time of the translocating head is expected to be on the order of 100 µs, (Veigel et al., 2002; Hinczewski et al., 2013) although the head spends tens of ms in the unbound state given the maximum rates of ATP hydrolysis and binding to actin (Veigel et al., 2002; Dunn and Spudich, 2007; Beausang et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: A 20 nm gold label was attached to the N-terminus of the myosin 5 head and tracked as the motor travels along actin filaments.
source: We attached a 20 nm gold label functioning as an efficient light scatterer to the N-terminus of the myosin 5 head and tracked its motion as the motor travels along actin filaments (Figure 1A, inset).
evidence: This claim describes the experimental methodology and is supported by the figure reference.

claim: Discrete 74 nm steps were observed at 1000 frames/s imaging speed with ∼4 nm positional precision.
source: From the centre of mass of the signal produced by the label, we determined the position of the head as a function of time revealing discrete 74 nm steps at 1000 frames/s imaging speed with ∼4 nm positional precision (Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, Video 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and figure references.

claim: The addition of the 20 nm label did not interfere with the mechano–chemical cycle of myosin 5a.
source: We verified that the addition of the 20 nm label did not interfere with the mechano–chemical cycle of myosin 5a by characterizing the speed of movement at different ATP concentrations.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental verification comparing with previous studies.

claim: The results compare well with those from a series of other single molecule studies where the molecule was labeled on the lever arm, the tail, or attached to a surface.
source: Our results compare well with those from a series of other single molecule studies where the molecule was labeled on the lever arm, the tail, or attached to a surface (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison with previous studies and figure reference.

claim: Periods of increased positional fluctuations were observed between detachment and reattachment of the labeled head.
source: In addition to the expected 74 nm steps, we observed periods of increased positional fluctuations between detachment and reattachment of the labeled head, previously interpreted as a signature of Brownian search (Dunn and Spudich, 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations and citation to previous interpretation.

claim: A transient state was revealed with a center of mass just over half way between the two binding sites and offset by 40 nm perpendicular to the actin filament.
source: Our effective lateral localization precision of 4 nm at 1000 frames/s, however, enabled us to visualize the motion of the unbound head precisely and revealed a transient state with a center of mass just over half way between the two binding sites and offset by 40 nm perpendicular to the actin filament (Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and figure reference.

claim: From the transient state position, the myosin head repeatedly moved back and forth between the next actin binding site and the transient state position.
source: From this position, the myosin head repeatedly moved back and forth between the next actin binding site and the transient state position (Figure 1C,D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations and figure references.

claim: The transient state represents a true potential minimum of the one head bound state of myosin.
source: On the rare occasions that the labelled leading head of myosin detached and reattached, it occupied a similar position in space to a translocating head (Figure 1—figure supplement 3), suggesting that the transient state represents a true potential minimum of the one head bound state of myosin.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from experimental observations.

claim: The iSCAT signal magnitude is very sensitive to the label-to-surface distance allowing for overall nanometric localization in three-dimensions.
source: In addition to providing nanometer precise information on the lateral position of the head through the center of mass of the signal, the iSCAT signal magnitude is very sensitive to the label-to-surface distance allowing for overall nanometric localization in three-dimensions (Krishnan et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work on iSCAT technique.

claim: The phase difference between scattered and reflected light fields changes according to the relation Φ = 4πηz/λ as the label moves perpendicular to the sample plane.
source: As the label moves perpendicular to the sample plane, the optical path length and with it the phase difference between the two fields changes by the following relation Φ = 4πηz/λ (Figure 2A, inset).
evidence: This claim is based on established optical principles and is illustrated in the figure.

claim: A complete signal inversion occurs for a displacement of z = λ/4η = 84 nm.
source: A complete signal inversion occurs for a displacement of z = λ/4η = 84 nm, where λ is the illumination wavelength (445 nm) and η the refractive index of the medium (1.33).
evidence: This claim is based on calculation from optical principles.

claim: Changes in contrast were often observed between the actin bound and unbound states.
source: We often observed these changes in contrast between the actin bound and unbound states (Figure 2A) and obtained an average change in iSCAT signal during the step (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations and figure references.

claim: The drop of 3.5% in iSCAT contrast suggests that the myosin head lifts on average by 24 ± 10 nm from its actin bound position.
source: The drop of 3.5% in iSCAT contrast (∼40% of the total signal) suggests that the myosin head lifts on average by 24 ± 10 nm from its actin bound position.
evidence: This claim is based on data analysis and inference from the iSCAT signal changes.

claim: In all recorded trajectories of doubly-labeled molecules that exhibited clear transient states in both the fluorescence and scattering channels, the transient states for both heads appeared on the same side of the actin filament.
source: In all recorded trajectories of doubly-labeled molecules that exhibited clear transient states in both the fluorescence and scattering channels, the transient states for both heads appeared on the same side of the actin filament (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from doubly-labeled molecules.

claim: A transition between two distinct states (AB transition) was frequently observed during each 74 nm step at 100 frames/s imaging speed.
source: At this imaging speed, we could frequently observe a transition between two distinct states during each 74 nm step in both an x–y projection (Figure 4A) and the time trace (Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations at improved temporal resolution.

claim: The AB transition involves a small, <10 nm, off-axis backward motion of the gold particle attached to the bound head.
source: As shown in the lateral trajectory, the transition between these states (AB transition) involves a small, <10 nm, off-axis backward motion of the gold particle attached to the bound head.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations.

claim: Sub-nm lateral localization precision was achieved for 20 nm gold at 100 frames/s.
source: The positional fluctuations (σ = 0.91 nm SD) of a surface-attached label recorded in the same field of view as the trajectory suggest that we achieved sub-nm lateral localization precision of 20 nm gold at 100 frames/s (Figure 4B, blue).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental measurements of a control sample.

claim: The localization noise increased for a gold bead attached to an actin-bound myosin (σ = 1.6 ± 0.3 nm) but remained small enough such that transitions on the order of 5 nm were clearly visible.
source: The localization noise increased for a gold bead attached to an actin-bound myosin (σ = 1.6 ± 0.3 nm in Figure 4B), but remained small enough such that transitions on the order of 5 nm were clearly visible (Figure 4A–B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental measurements.

claim: A clear drop in the iSCAT contrast was observed when the labeled trailing head detached and transitioned to the leading position.
source: We observed a clear drop in the iSCAT contrast when the labeled trailing head detached and transitioned to the leading position (Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations.

claim: A much smaller change in iSCAT contrast was measured during the AB transition, likely due to a three-dimensional reorientation of the label.
source: We also measured a much smaller change in iSCAT contrast during the AB transition, likely due to a three-dimensional reorientation of the label.
evidence: This claim is based on experimental observation and inference about the cause.

claim: Both the large-scale translocation of the head and the subsequent smaller backwards transition coincide with translation of the tail.
source: The resulting traces showed that both the large-scale translocation of the head and the subsequent smaller backwards transition coincide with translation of the tail (Figure 5A).
evidence: This claim is supported by simultaneous tracking of head and tail.

claim: The small-scale transition accompanies the power stroke of the attached labeled head (AB transition) and is representative of a pre- to post-power stroke transition.
source: This implies that the small-scale transition accompanies the power stroke of the attached labeled head (AB transition) and is representative of a pre- to post-power stroke transition (Figure 5B).
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the simultaneous tracking data.

claim: The average size of the AB transition increased from 7.4 ± 3.2 nm to 9.5 ± 3.1 nm and 11.5 ± 2.5 nm for 20, 30 and 40 nm diameter labels, respectively.
source: We found that the average size of the AB transition increased from 7.4 ± 3.2 nm to 9.5 ± 3.1 nm and 11.5 ± 2.5 nm for 20, 30 and 40 nm diameter labels, respectively (Figure 6A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data using different sized labels.

claim: The AB transition reports on a conformational change of the bound head, which is a rotation of the N-terminal domain, rather than a translation of the head itself along actin.
source: This suggests that the AB transition reports on a conformational change of the bound head, which is a rotation of the N-terminal domain, rather than a translation of the head itself along actin.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the label size-dependent data.

claim: Using the model and data, an angle of rotation α = 20° and a distance x = 1.7 nm were obtained.
source: Using the hydrodynamic radii for the labels obtained by dynamic light scattering (20, 26 and 32 nm), we obtained α = 20° for the angle and x = 1.7 nm.
evidence: This claim is based on data analysis using a geometric model.

claim: Trajectories recorded at 100 frames/s frequently showed both the position of the transient state and the direction of the AB transition, revealing that they were invariably in line.
source: Trajectories recorded at 100 frames/s frequently showed both the position of the transient state and the direction of the AB transition, revealing that they were invariably in line (Figure 7A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations.

claim: During the recording of 351 traces that exhibited clear signatures of the transient state at 100 frames/s, a preference (66% vs 33%) of right over left-handed walking was found.
source: During the recording of 351 traces that exhibited clear signatures of the transient state at 100 frames/s, we found a preference (66% vs 33%) of right over left-handed walking.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: Within individual traces, the transient state was only observed on the same side of actin.
source: Within individual traces, we only observed the transient state on the same side of actin.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations.

claim: For 102 switching events, the transient state remained on the same side of the filament 60% of the time, while changing sides in 40% of the events.
source: For 102 switching events, we found that the transient state remained on the same side of the filament 60% of the time, while changing sides in 40% of the events.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: The dwell time of the transient state followed a single exponential distribution with a lifetime of 17.5 ± 0.6 ms.
source: We found that it followed a single exponential distribution with a lifetime of 17.5 ± 0.6 ms.
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of experimental dwell time data.

claim: No ATP concentration dependence was found on both the spatial and temporal distributions of the transient state within experimental error.
source: We found no ATP concentration dependence on both the spatial and temporal distributions of the transient state within our experimental error (Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data at different ATP concentrations.

claim: The dwell times of the A and the B states were identical suggesting that the 20 nm gold particle had no effect on the stepping kinetics.
source: In all cases, the dwell times of the A and the B states were identical suggesting that the 20 nm gold particle had no effect on the stepping kinetics.
evidence: This claim is based on analysis of dwell time data and inference about label effects.

claim: The 20 nm gold particle attached to the N-terminus of myosin has no measureable effect on the kinetics of stepping.
source: By monitoring the lifetimes of the A and B states, which effectively provides the dwell times of the labeled and unlabeled heads, respectively, we demonstrate that the 20 nm gold particle attached to the N-terminus of myosin has no measureable effect on the kinetics of stepping.
evidence: This claim is based on experimental verification of dwell times.

claim: The label probes the structural change occurring in the bound head during the power stroke and amplifies it into a nanometer scale motion.
source: Here, the label probes the structural change occurring in the bound head during the power stroke and amplifies it into a nanometer scale motion.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental observations with different sized labels.

claim: Previous studies using gold labels were not able to observe the AB transition likely due to a combination of a different labeling strategy and much lower spatial precision.
source: Previous studies using gold labels were not able to observe this transition likely due to a combination of a different labeling strategy (40 nm or 60 nm gold nanoparticle attached to a calmodulin on the lever arm) and much lower spatial precision (>10 nm) (Dunn and Spudich, 2007).
evidence: This claim is based on comparison with previous studies and inference about methodological differences.

claim: Several EM studies failed to detect any obvious conformational differences in the position of the SH3 (N-terminal domain) of lead and trail heads.
source: Several EM studies (Walker et al., 2000; Burgess et al., 2002; Oke et al., 2010) failed to detect any obvious conformational differences in the position of the SH3 (N-terminal domain) of lead and trail heads, whereas we now demonstrate a movement of this domain associated with the power stroke taken after the trail head dissociates.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous EM studies.

claim: The N-terminus undergoes a rotation during the power stroke transition according to molecular dynamic simulations of both myosin 5a and myosin 2 based on crystal structures.
source: This change is consistent with results of molecular dynamic simulations of both myosin 5a and myosin 2 based on crystal structures suggesting that the N-terminus undergoes a rotation during the power stroke transition (Coureux et al., 2003; Cecchini et al., 2008; Preller and Holmes, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to computational studies.

claim: During the acquisition of 4728 steps in 635 trajectories, 64–10 nm sub-steps were never observed.
source: During the acquisition of 4728 steps in 635 trajectories, we never observed a large followed by a small forward step.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of a large dataset.

claim: Myosin remains firmly bound to actin with both heads during the mechanochemical cycle irrespective of whether the head is leading or trailing, except when the head takes a 74 nm step.
source: The sensitivity of our tracking methodology to detachment from actin in three dimensions, however, shows that myosin remains firmly bound to actin with both heads during the mechanochemical cycle irrespective of whether the head is leading or trailing (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), except when the head takes a 74 nm step.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations.

claim: Only ~3% of steps taken at 1 µM ATP, ~0.6% of steps taken at 10 µM ATP, and none at saturating ATP exhibited leading head detachment.
source: Specifically, only ~3% of steps taken at 1 µM ATP, ~0.6% of steps taken at 10 µM ATP, none at saturating ATP exhibited this behavior.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: The transient state lifetime agrees with the duration of increased flexibility reported in optical trapping experiments probing the attachment stiffness at high time-resolution.
source: The transient state lifetime agrees with the duration of increased flexibility reported in optical trapping experiments probing the attachment stiffness at high time-resolution (Veigel et al., 2002) and single molecule tracking of the motor domain (Dunn and Spudich, 2007; Beausang et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is based on comparison with previous studies.

claim: The measured lifetime correlates well with previously reported ensemble rate constant for the weak-to-strong binding transition (47 s−1).
source: The measured lifetime also correlates well with previously reported ensemble rate constant for the weak-to-strong binding transition (47 s−1) (Rosenfeld and Sweeney, 2004).
evidence: This claim is based on comparison with previous ensemble measurements.

claim: The position of the transient state, displaced 40 nm along and perpendicular to the filament is inconsistent with a purely rotational diffusion search.
source: An important implication of our data is that the position of the transient state, displaced 40 nm along and perpendicular to the filament is inconsistent with a purely rotational diffusion search.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data and comparison with theoretical expectations.

claim: The intrinsic angle between the lever arms is similar to that found when the two heads are bound to actin, that is, ∼37 nm away from each other.
source: This location and the resulting movement, however, become more intuitive when considering that the intrinsic angle between the lever arms is similar to that found when the two heads are bound to actin, that is, ∼37 nm away from each other.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from structural considerations.

claim: Comparison of electron micrographs of myosin 5 bound to actin and non-specifically bound to a surface in the absence of actin show clearly peaked angle distributions around 105 and 115°, respectively.
source: Comparison of electron micrographs of myosin 5 bound to actin (Walker et al., 2000) and non-specifically bound to a surface in the absence of actin (Takagi et al., 2014) show clearly peaked angle distributions around 105 and 115°, respectively, suggesting a built-in preference for such a spatial arrangement of the two heads, rather than a truly flexible linkage, another indication that a completely free swivel at the neck-linker is unlikely.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to EM studies and inference about structural constraints.

claim: Myosin side steps along actin in a combined twisting and leaning motion, much more like a drawing compass rather than a freely jointed swivel or human-like gait.
source: The position of the transient state together with what appears to be constrained diffusion suggests that myosin side steps along actin in a combined twisting and leaning motion, much more like a drawing compass rather than a freely jointed swivel or human-like gait.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental observations of the transient state position and dynamics.

claim: The AB transition and the relative location of the rear-binding site and the transient state are in line.
source: The fact that the AB transition and the relative location of the rear-binding site and the transient state are in line has two further important implications.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations.

claim: The AB transition cannot solely be a consequence of a steric interaction between the label and the lever arm.
source: It suggests that the AB transition cannot solely be a consequence of a steric interaction between the label and the lever arm. In that case, we should only observe one type of AB transition, irrespective of whether right or left-handed walking occurs.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the observation that AB transition direction correlates with transient state position.

claim: Myosin walks in a symmetric manner where each head movement is accompanied by an 180° swing on the same side of the actin filament.
source: The simultaneous tracking of the movement of both heads using the combination of gold scattering and fluorescence demonstrates that myosin walks in a symmetric manner where each head movement is accompanied by an 180° swing on the same side of the actin filament, unlike a human gait.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from simultaneous tracking of both heads.

claim: The orientation of the transient state relative to actin may change for the same molecule by binding to another actin filament.
source: Our observation that the orientation of the transient state relative to actin may change for the same molecule by binding to another actin filament shows that the position of the transient state relative to actin is not an intrinsic property of individual myosin molecules.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations of filament switching events.

claim: The decision about transient state orientation is made upon binding to actin, with both cases following the right and left hand preference previously mentioned.
source: Instead, the decision is made upon binding to actin, with both cases following the right and left hand preference previously mentioned.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the filament switching observations.

claim: The twisting that takes place during the initial binding event of both heads to actin determines the directionality.
source: Based on our observation that the transient state for both heads occurs on the same side of the actin filament we propose that the twisting that takes place during the initial binding event of both heads to actin determines the directionality.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on inference from experimental observations.

claim: Rabbit skeletal muscle actin was prepared as described by Spudich and Watt, 1971.
source: Rabbit skeletal muscle actin was prepared as described (Spudich and Watt, 1971) and stored in liquid nitrogen until used.
evidence: This is a methodological statement supported by citation.

claim: Mouse myosin 5a HMM with a C-terminal GFP was expressed in the presence of calmodulin and purified as described by Wang, 2000.
source: Mouse myosin 5a HMM with a C-terminal GFP was expressed in the presence of calmodulin and purified as described (Wang, 2000).
evidence: This is a methodological statement supported by citation.

claim: The N-terminus was modified by the addition of a nucleotide sequence encoding an AviTag peptide for site-specific biotinylation with BirA ligase.
source: In addition, the N-terminus was modified by the addition of a nucleotide sequence encoding an AviTag peptide (GLNDIFEAQKIEWHE) for site-specific biotinylation with BirA ligase (Avidity, Aurora, Colorado).
evidence: This is a methodological statement describing sample preparation.

claim: Gold nanoparticles of 20 nm, 30 nm and 40 nm in diameter conjugated with streptavidin were purchased from BBI (UK).
source: Gold nanoparticles of 20 nm, 30 nm and 40 nm in diameter conjugated with streptavidin were purchased from BBI (UK) and directly mixed with biotinylated myosin 5a sample in a 4:1, gold to myosin ratio, consistent with one or zero myosin molecules per gold particle.
evidence: This is a methodological statement describing materials and sample preparation.

claim: Interferometric scattering microscopy was performed as detailed previously by Ortega-Arroyo and Kukura, 2012.
source: Interferometric scattering microscopy was performed as detailed previously (Ortega-Arroyo and Kukura, 2012).
evidence: This is a methodological statement supported by citation.

claim: The incident power was adjusted to 17.9 kW/cm2 at the sample to achieve near-saturation of the CMOS camera, which ensured shot noise limited detection.
source: The incident power was adjusted to 17.9 kW/cm2 at the sample to achieve near-saturation of the CMOS camera, which ensured shot noise limited detection.
evidence: This is a methodological statement describing experimental conditions.
